steps.caption: goose starts in a repository and reads AGENTS.md for the project’s standing instructions.
When a task matches one, it loads an Agent Skill: a folder of instructions and scripts.
Its tools arrive as extensions, which are based on MCP.
One of those servers can be OpenSandbox, so the agent runs commands in an isolated sandbox.
OpenSandbox’s CLI can also install its own skills as SKILL.md files, so a coding agent learns how to drive the sandbox. Its install targets are Claude, Codex, opencode and others; goose is not named.
An agent starts the trip: Agent Router ships an example that sends goose’s model calls and MCP tool calls through one gateway. The example still uses the old name, Envoy AI Gateway.
Agent Router gives applications one OpenAI-compatible API to every model…
…and to MCP servers, behind the same front door.
It can carry A2A traffic too, through a preview guide; there is no dedicated A2A route type yet.
agentgateway also routes traffic to LLM providers…
…federates tools over MCP…
…and carries agent-to-agent traffic over A2A.
The two now overlap on models and MCP, and both document A2A. Agent Router cites agentgateway’s design, but no AAIF document draws the line between them.
MCP deepens one agent with tools. A2A connects that agent to other agents.
agentgateway documents A2A as a gateway feature…
…and Agent Router documents a preview way to route A2A agents through it.
In training, an agent acts in an OpenEnv environment through step().

In production, the same environment serves its tools over /mcp. OpenEnv’s RFC 003, still in review, says this reuses its own HTTP transport with MCP’s JSON-RPC message format, and that standard Streamable HTTP is planned.
An application sends one request shape, defined by Open Responses…
…and any provider that implements it can answer.
The spec names MCP once, as an example of tools hosted on external servers. It defines no MCP tool type.
